label: Concert grand pianos, close mics, dry
audition_title: libsonare piano vs the sampled reference
_dry: Every effect section the plugin advertises is switched off, so no reverberation is added to what the samples hold. That is a statement about the plugin and not about the recording: see _floor.
_floor: The samples carry about -64 dBFS of rumble, which plays back with them and is therefore absent from the lead-in and present under every note. Measured on a held C4 three to five seconds after note-off: 5-20 Hz reads -64.4, -63.4 and -64.2 dBFS on the three instruments -- within a decibel of each other, which is one recording chain rather than three pianos -- and it survives both a -92 dB-sidelobe window and a brick-wall lowpass at 375 Hz that removes the note entirely, so it is the recording and not spectral leakage. Nothing radiates at eight hertz, so the level is a floor by construction. Consequence: below roughly 250 Hz this corpus cannot say what the tail should be, and a band comparison there measures the floor. `shape takes` refuses those bands; a fit that is allowed to reach them walks its controls to their bounds.
_late_top: Above C6 the held-note DECAY readings in the reference profile are fitted mostly over a bed this corpus cannot attribute. Measured on the 10 ms windowed envelope: a C8 falls about 48 dB from its peak inside one second and then sits near -77 dB for a second and a half before wandering down, so `decay_db_s` and `decay_late_db_s` there are read over roughly 4.4 s of which the last 3.4 s is that bed, and what comes back is close to (peak - bed) / gate length. Whether the bed is the instrument is NOT settled: the level a note settles at should move with the blow, and at C4 it moves 23 dB across v24 to v120 on all three instruments, while at C7 and C8 it moves 1.7 dB on grand-227 and 8.3 on grand-274 -- and 23 on grand-290, which keeps its separation the whole way. Two instruments say floor and one says instrument, so the reading is left as measured and flagged rather than corrected. DECAY_RANGE_DB cannot exclude it: the bed sits 48 dB under the peak and the bound is 60. Consequence: a top-octave decay or aftersound delta is weak evidence in either direction, and a model whose C8 matches the reference rate may be matching a recording. The first-crossing span -- how long the note takes to fall 40 dB the FIRST time -- is not affected and reads 0.43 to 0.54 s on all three.
_late_bed: The AFTERSOUND readings are not the string above the middle of the keyboard, and unlike `_late_top` this is not confined to the top octave. `decay_late_db_s` is flat across the whole instrument on all three: every note from A0 to C8 reads between -1.4 and -5.1 dB/s, with no trend. Read instead on the note's own on-partial rows, over windows centred at 0.65, 2.25 and 5.0 s, the same three carry an unmistakable taper they agree on to within their own 0.4-to-3.6 dB/s disagreement: median -4.5 at A0, -6.3 at C4, -6.8 at C6, -13.4 at C7 and -12.8 at C8. The flat reading is not just different, it is impossible -- -3 dB/s at C8 is a note still sounding fifteen seconds after the strike, and this same capture puts C8's first 40 dB fall at 0.43 to 0.50 s. A third angle shows the two apart in opposite directions at once: at F#6 `decay_span_s` has the reference outlasting the model 7.3 s to 3.6, while the first-crossing span has the model outlasting the reference 2.14 s to 0.95. Both are true. The reference falls fast and then stops falling, onto something that is not the note -- `_floor` prices the recording's own share of it and `_above_fundamental` in profile.py names the rest, the case and board ringing at the same 21, 35 and 82 Hz under every note alike. Consequence: a taper fitted to this dimension comes out too slow, and correcting the voice against the partials instead makes the dimension read WORSE while the late on-partial level error over C6 to C8 falls from 10-34 dB to 0.3-4.3. The remedy is the one the release measurement already uses -- cut below the fundamental before reading the envelope -- and applying it here re-measures four instruments' references and re-records their gates.
_host: Measured by `capture.py calibrate`, not chosen. Without realtime this plugin drops 1544 ms out of the middle of a 2 s note; at settle 1000 it renders a peak of 0.0011 and at 2000 the real 0.158. The recommendation is twice the measured minimum.
_stimulus: A long gate and a short tail, because on a piano note-off is the damper: the free decay a model has to match happens while the key is still down, and everything after it is the damping. Eight seconds covers the double-decay knee, which arrives one to three seconds in.
_timbres: Three concert grands of increasing scale length, close-miked, one preset each from that instrument's own close folder. Length rather than name because length is the property the measurements answer to: it sets the bass string's stiffness and so the inharmonicity curve the profile reports.
_dimensions: One exclusion, measured rather than assumed. `damper` is out because the capture cannot hold enough of one: a grand's release does not fall 40 dB inside the 2 s tail at low velocity, and above the middle the string has already stopped before the key comes up, so only 14 to 27 rows of 60 carry a release on any one instrument and only 11 to 18 are shared by any two. On those the three grands disagree with each other by 120 to 195 ms at the median and by more than 900 ms at the worst note — wider than the model's own error — so a bound recorded here fails on which instrument it was compared against rather than on anything the voice did. Lengthen `tail` and re-measure before gating it. `tnr` is out for now for a different reason: the column reaches the summary, but nothing has yet measured whether the three grands agree on it, and a bound recorded before that says more about which instrument it was compared against than about the voice. The rest are gated, including four that no other column here can see: the envelope's time to peak, which on a piano is the soundboard's bloom rather than the hammer; the width between the two radiation paths, which is exactly 0.0 for a model that folds one signal into both legs; the aftersound, the second and much slower decay rate a string falls to once its unison has drifted out of phase; and the gap between that rate and the prompt one, which is the size of the double decay itself. The last two are what a straight-line `decay` fit is actively blind to rather than merely silent about — the single slope lands between the two regimes, so a voice can hold it while having three times the grands' late rate at C5, which is what this one did, and a voice with no double decay at all holds every one of the other three by putting the same rate in both stages.
_dimensions_na: The exclusions above, as data. Coverage is read against `toneclass.canonical_dimensions`, and a canonical dimension is either gated, or excused here with its reason, or a gap — so an exclusion argued only in prose reads as a gap however good the argument.

dimensions_na.damper: the three grands disagree by 120-195 ms at the median, wider than the model's own error
dimensions_na.tnr: the column reaches the summary, but nothing has measured whether the three grands agree on it

_notes: The two extremes of the keyboard plus every sixth semitone between C1 and C7. The extremes are in because they are where a physical model diverges most: A0 is three wound strings with a wildly inharmonic partial series, C8 is a single short string with almost no sustain.
_velocities: Four points, wide apart. A piano's timbre changes more with velocity than with pitch, so this axis carries most of the information a brightness-versus-loudness model needs.
_identity: Which product this was captured from lives in the untracked sibling `piano.local.json`: the plugin's component triple and each timbre's preset. Everything here is the method. Re-capturing needs the overlay; scoring, fitting and diagnosing read `reference/piano.json` and need nothing.
